chapters.caption: The Tower from the Thames — White Tower at the centre, Traitors' Gate below
chapters.directions: Enter via the Middle Byward Gate at the southwest corner. Once inside, resist the urge to wander — head straight ahead, past the White Tower on your right, toward the Waterloo Barracks along the north wall for the Crown Jewels.
chapters.text: Start outside the walls if you can, down by the river, and just look at it for a moment. That pale stone keep rising in the middle — the White Tower — was already old when half the buildings of Europe were timber. William the Conqueror began it around 1078, barely a decade after he'd conquered England, and the message was not subtle: a stone fortress, in a city of wooden houses, planted right at London's gate. I'm here to stay. Over the next 900 years, his successors wrapped it in two rings of walls and a moat, and the Tower became the Swiss Army knife of English monarchy — palace, fortress, treasury, prison, mint, zoo, and execution ground. Three queens of England lost their heads here. Two little princes vanished here, in the most famous unsolved mystery in British history. And the Crown Jewels — the actual crowns worn at coronations — still live here, guarded around the clock. As you come in through the Middle Byward Gate, notice you're crossing what was once a water-filled moat. And keep perspective: for all its dark fame, only a handful of executions happened inside these walls. The Tower's terror was mostly reputation — which, as you'll see, was quite enough.
chapters.title: Welcome to the Tower

chapters.caption: The Imperial State Crown — worn by the monarch at the State Opening of Parliament
chapters.directions: The Jewel House is inside the Waterloo Barracks, the long 19th-century building along the north wall. Exit, and turn right (east), then head back south toward the White Tower in the centre of the grounds.
chapters.text: Head straight here, before anything else — this is why we came in early. The Crown Jewels are not museum replicas. This is the working regalia of the British monarchy, still taken out and used: the Imperial State Crown leaves this vault every year for the State Opening of Parliament. The exhibition walks you through coronation film and ceremony first — watch for the sheer choreography of it — and then you step onto a moving walkway that glides you past the crowns themselves. Look for St Edward's Crown, the heavy gold crown used at the actual moment of coronation, worn only once in a monarch's reign. Then the Imperial State Crown: nearly 3,000 diamonds, and set into it, a who's-who of famous stones — the Black Prince's Ruby (actually a spinel, worn by Henry V at Agincourt), the Stuart Sapphire, and Cullinan II, the second-largest stone cut from the biggest diamond ever found. And find the Sovereign's Sceptre with the Cross: on top sits Cullinan I, the Great Star of Africa, at 530 carats the largest clear-cut diamond in the world. One honest warning: the walkway keeps you moving. If you want a second, slower look, just loop around and ride it again — nobody minds. No photos in here, so take your time and actually look.
chapters.title: The Crown Jewels — Go First

chapters.caption: The White Tower (c. 1078) — London's original Norman keep
chapters.directions: Exit the White Tower and head east to the Salt Tower, where stairs take you up onto the Inner Wall Walk (the Battlements).
chapters.text: Now for the building that gives the whole place its name. The White Tower is the oldest complete Norman keep in England — begun around 1078, built of pale stone imported from Caen in Normandy, and whitewashed in 1240, which is how it got its name. For over 200 years this was the tallest building in London. You enter, as medieval visitors did, up an external stair to the first floor — defenders could chop the wooden steps away behind them. Work your way up to St John's Chapel, and stop. This little chapel, from about 1080, is one of the purest Norman interiors in Europe: round arches, thick barrel vault, almost no decoration — and somehow more moving for it. Kings prayed here; prisoners awaited their fate here. Then explore the Royal Armouries floors. The star is the Line of Kings — a parade of armours worn by monarchs, first arranged in the 1600s as a piece of royal propaganda. Find Henry VIII's foot-combat armour from 1540: a gleaming ton of steel engineering, and yes, everyone notices the codpiece — it's meant to be noticed. Compare it with the much slimmer armour Henry wore as a young man; the two suits together tell the story of a king's expanding waistline more honestly than any portrait. Don't miss the executioner's block and axe on this floor either — grim, real, and quietly displayed.
chapters.title: The White Tower — St John's Chapel, the Line of Kings, and Henry VIII's Armour

chapters.caption: The Wall Walk along the inner curtain wall, looking toward Tower Bridge
chapters.directions: Follow the Wall Walk south and west. It delivers you toward the Wakefield and Lanthorn Towers — the Medieval Palace — on the south wall above the river.
chapters.text: Climb up here and get your bearings — this is the best orientation point in the Tower. You're standing on the inner curtain wall, much of it built by Henry III and Edward I in the 1200s as they turned William's keep into a concentric fortress: a castle inside a castle, so attackers who breached one wall faced another. Walk slowly and look both ways. Outward: the grassy moat (once filled with Thames water, and famously smelly), the outer wall, and beyond it, Tower Bridge doing its best to look medieval — it's actually Victorian, from 1894, and we'll cross it later. Inward: the whole geometry of the place makes sense from up here — White Tower in the middle, Tower Green below, the river sliding past Traitors' Gate. The small towers you'll pass along this walk each have a job and a story: they served as lookout posts, stores, lodgings, and — as the wall became a prison — cells for prisoners important enough to keep comfortably and securely. Look for the reconstructions of defensive features as you go: portcullis grooves, arrow slits angled for crossfire, and the sheer drop designed into every approach. Medieval military engineering wasn't decorative. Every quirk up here exists because somebody, at some point, tried to get in.
chapters.title: The Battlements — Walking the Wall Walk

chapters.caption: The Wakefield Tower chamber, centrepiece of the Medieval Palace
chapters.directions: From the Lanthorn Tower, continue west along the inner wall to the Bloody Tower, just north of Traitors' Gate.
chapters.text: Come down off the wall into the Wakefield and Lanthorn Towers, and suddenly the fortress turns into a home. This is the Medieval Palace, built mainly for Henry III and Edward I in the 1200s, and the rooms have been re-created to show how a medieval king actually lived when he stayed here — which was often, especially in troubled times, because the Tower was the safest address in London. In the Wakefield Tower, look for the king's great chamber: a throne under a canopy, painted decoration, and a private oratory — a tiny prayer room tucked off the main space. Medieval kingship ran on ceremony and piety in about equal measure, and this one room shows both. Notice the details that made it liveable: a real fireplace (a luxury), garderobe — that's a medieval toilet — and windows positioned to catch light while staying defensible. Edward I's bedchamber in the Lanthorn Tower gives you the domestic end of it: a great bed, chests for the royal wardrobe that travelled with the king, and wall paintings re-created from medieval patterns. It's easy to tour the Tower as pure prison-and-execution theatre. These rooms are the corrective. For most of its life, this was a working royal residence — the king's furniture, clerks, and household moved in and out, and state business was done right here.
chapters.title: The Medieval Palace — How Kings Actually Lived

chapters.caption: The Bloody Tower — last home of the two princes, Edward V and Richard of York
chapters.directions: Before moving on, glance down at Traitors' Gate on the river wall below — prisoners arrived by boat through this water gate. Then head north across Tower Green to the chapel.
chapters.text: This tower's original name was the Garden Tower — it overlooked the Lieutenant's garden. It earned its current name from the darkest cold case in English history. In 1483, King Edward IV died, and his 12-year-old son was proclaimed Edward V. The boy king and his 9-year-old brother, Richard, were lodged here in the Tower — normal practice while a coronation was prepared. Their uncle, Richard, Duke of Gloucester, had himself declared protector, then declared the boys illegitimate, then took the throne as Richard III. The princes were seen playing in the grounds that summer. Then they were seen less. Then not at all. They were never seen alive again. No bodies were produced, no trial, no announcement — just silence, and a mystery that has run for over 540 years. Did Richard III order their murder, as Shakespeare insists? Or was it Henry VII, who beat Richard at Bosworth and had his own reasons? In 1674, workmen demolishing a staircase in the White Tower found a wooden box containing the skeletons of two children, roughly the right ages. Charles II had them reburied in Westminster Abbey, where they remain — and where, despite modern DNA science, they remain untested by royal permission. Stand here a moment. Whatever happened, it happened within a few yards of where you're standing.
chapters.title: The Bloody Tower — The Princes in the Tower

chapters.caption: Tower Green and the Chapel Royal of St Peter ad Vincula
chapters.directions: From the chapel, walk east along the north side of the Green to the Beauchamp Tower, in the northwest stretch of the inner wall.
chapters.text: This quiet patch of grass is the most charged ground in the Tower. The glass-and-stone memorial in the middle marks the scaffold site where, in front of small invited crowds, seven people were beheaded — among them two queens of England. Anne Boleyn died here on 19 May 1536, executed on charges of adultery and treason that most historians now consider fabricated. She'd asked — and Henry VIII had agreed, in a final twisted courtesy — for a swordsman from Calais rather than the clumsy English axe. Contemporary accounts say she kept her nerve and her wit to the end, remarking that she had 'a little neck.' Five years later her cousin Catherine Howard, Henry's fifth wife, followed her to the same scaffold, aged about 19. And in 1554, the 'nine days' queen,' Lady Jane Grey — a teenager used as a pawn by ambitious men — was executed here too. Most Tower executions actually happened publicly on Tower Hill, outside the walls; a private death on the Green was, perversely, a privilege of rank. Now step into the Chapel of St Peter ad Vincula, just beside the Green. Anne, Catherine, and Jane are all buried under its floor, near the altar — identified when the chapel was restored in Victorian times. It's still a working chapel, and its plainness is the point. After the theatre of the scaffold, this is where the Tower keeps its dead, quietly.
chapters.title: Tower Green and St Peter ad Vincula — Anne Boleyn's Resting Place

chapters.caption: Prisoner graffiti carved into the Beauchamp Tower walls
chapters.directions: Continue around the inner wall to the Bell Tower and the Royal Beasts exhibition area on the west side, near the entrance.
chapters.text: If you only linger in one small tower, make it this one — and bring your eyes close to the walls. The Beauchamp Tower (say 'Beecham') was a prime cell for high-status prisoners in Tudor times, and its residents had time, tools, and a desperate need to be remembered. So they carved. There are around 90 inscriptions here, and they're extraordinary: names, dates, prayers, coats of arms, and elaborate emblems cut deep into the stone. Find the carving by John Dudley, Earl of Warwick, from 1553–54: he and his brothers were imprisoned after their father tried to put Lady Jane Grey on the throne. John carved his family emblem — the bear and ragged staff — surrounded by flowers for each brother, with a verse hoping the carvings would outlast them. He died shortly after his release; the carving did outlast him, by nearly five centuries now. Look too for the poignant inscription of Philip Howard, Earl of Arundel, a Catholic prisoner of Elizabeth I, and the simple scratched crosses and 'IHS' monograms of men measuring out their last weeks in stone. Remember, these weren't vandals — carving was permitted, sometimes even encouraged. For a prisoner facing execution with no tomb guaranteed, a name in the wall was a bid for exactly what you're giving it right now: to not be forgotten.
chapters.title: The Beauchamp Tower — Prisoner Graffiti

chapters.caption: Wire sculptures recall the lions, elephants and polar bears of the Royal Menagerie
chapters.directions: Walk toward the Middle Tower area and look for the Tower Mint exhibition along the outer wall, east of the entrance.
chapters.text: Here's the chapter nobody expects: for about 600 years, the Tower of London was also London's zoo. From the 1200s, foreign rulers sent exotic animals as diplomatic gifts, and the Royal Menagerie housed them at the Tower's western entrance — which is why the tower there is still called the Lion Tower. Henry III started the serious collecting: three leopards (the gift, and the origin of the lions on England's coat of arms confusion), an African elephant in 1255 — the first seen in England since Roman times, drawn from life by the chronicler Matthew Paris — and a polar bear, also from the King of Norway, which was famously allowed to swim and fish in the Thames on a long chain. Imagine commuting past that. The wire animal sculptures you'll see around the site mark where the menagerie animals lived. Life for them was rough — cramped cages, strange diets, and crowds poking them with sticks, which occasionally ended badly for the crowds. A lion named after whoever was fashionable, monkeys, zebras, even kangaroos by the 1700s. By the 1820s the menagerie had become a popular public attraction, but welfare concerns and one too many escaped-animal incidents led the Duke of Wellington to close it in the 1830s. The animals moved to Regent's Park — and became the founding collection of London Zoo.
chapters.title: Royal Beasts — The Tower Menagerie

chapters.caption: A shilling struck at the Tower Mint — for 500 years England's coins were made inside these walls
chapters.directions: Continue to the Lower Wakefield Tower, on the south inner wall near the Medieval Palace, for the Torture at the Tower exhibition.
chapters.text: Money needs guarding, so for over 500 years England made its money in the safest place in the kingdom: right here, along the street now called Mint Street, inside the Tower's outer wall. From about 1279 until 1810, nearly every English coin passed through this lane. The exhibition here walks you through how brutal and skilled the work was: silver and gold arrived under guard, was melted, rolled, cut into blanks, and struck — originally by a man with a hammer and a die, one coin at a time. Get the weight of that: a good moneyer struck thousands of coins a day, by hand, and woe betide him if the weight was off — clipping and debasing coinage were treason, punished accordingly. The Mint's most famous master? Isaac Newton. Yes, that Newton. After revolutionising physics, he ran the Mint from 1696, professionalised it, and personally hunted counterfeiters through London's underworld with terrifying zeal — several forgers went to the gallows on his evidence. Look for displays on the Great Recoinage, when Newton oversaw replacing England's entire battered currency. By 1810 the Mint had outgrown the Tower and moved to a purpose-built steam-powered factory nearby; the Royal Mint eventually ended up in Wales, where it still makes Britain's coins. The money left. The walls that protected it are the ones you're walking through.
chapters.title: The Tower Mint — Where England's Money Was Made

chapters.caption: The Lower Wakefield Tower — home of the 'Torture at the Tower' exhibition
chapters.directions: Head back out to Tower Green, where the ravens are usually to be found near their enclosure on the south side of the Green.
chapters.text: Down in the Lower Wakefield Tower you'll find the Tower's most deliberately unsettling exhibition — and it's worth saying up front that it corrects as much myth as it confirms. Torture was real here, but it was rare, and it was bureaucratically controlled: under the Tudors and early Stuarts, torture in England required a specific warrant from the Privy Council, and the Tower's records show it was authorised only a few dozen times over more than a century. The exhibition displays the instruments associated with that grim system. There's the rack, which stretched the body until joints dislocated — Guy Fawkes was racked after the Gunpowder Plot of 1605, and you can see his signature on his confession, firm before torture and a shaky scrawl after. There are the manacles, in which prisoners were suspended by the wrists, and the Scavenger's Daughter, a hoop of iron that did the opposite of the rack, crushing the body into a ball. The most famous victim of the rack here may be Anne Askew, a Protestant writer racked in 1546 — illegally, since torturing a gentlewoman required special authority — and so badly injured she had to be carried to her execution at Smithfield. The tone of this little exhibition is, to its credit, sober rather than sensational. Read the panels: the real horror isn't the ironwork, it's the paperwork — torture by warrant, signed and filed.
chapters.title: Torture at the Tower — The Lower Wakefield Tower

chapters.caption: A Tower raven on Tower Green — legend says the kingdom falls if they leave
chapters.directions: From Tower Green, make your way to the exit the way you came in, past the Middle Byward Gate — or detour down to the river wall for a last look at Traitors' Gate.
chapters.text: Time for the Tower's most beloved residents. There are at least six ravens here at all times — that's the rule, and there's usually a spare or two — and according to legend, this is not optional: if the ravens ever leave the Tower, the Crown will fall, and Britain with it. The story is usually credited to Charles II, who supposedly wanted the ravens removed because they interfered with the royal astronomer's telescope, was warned of the prophecy, and compromised: the telescope moved to Greenwich, the ravens stayed, and they've been on the payroll — officially enlisted, fed at public expense — ever since. Historians suspect the legend is largely a Victorian invention, but try telling that to the Ravenmaster, the Yeoman Warder whose full-time job is caring for these birds. Look at them closely: ravens are huge — a wingspan over a metre — glossy, clever, and fully aware they run the place. They eat raw meat, biscuits soaked in blood, and the occasional pilfered sandwich; each has a name and a personality, and the Ravenmaster's talks (check the daily programme) are full of stories of individual birds' mischief. Their wings are lightly trimmed on one side so they stay close — they can fly around the grounds but not away. The kingdom, you'll be relieved to hear, is safe.
chapters.title: The Ravens — Guardians of the Kingdom

chapters.caption: The White Tower above Tower Green — the heart of the fortress
chapters.directions: Exit via the Middle Byward Gate. For Tower Bridge, turn left (east) outside the walls and follow the Thames Path about 10 minutes.
chapters.text: As you head for the gate, take one last look back at the White Tower, and consider what this place has managed to be. It has been the seat of kings and the death place of queens. It has held the Crown Jewels, the national treasury, the Royal Mint, a zoo, an observatory, and some of the most famous prisoners in history — including, for a while, a future queen: Elizabeth I was imprisoned here by her sister Mary, entering through Traitors' Gate in 1554, convinced she was going to die. She walked out, became queen, and — tellingly — came back to the Tower the night before her coronation, as tradition demanded. That's the Tower in one story: the place you entered as a prisoner could be the place you left as a monarch. It stopped being a royal residence centuries ago, but it never stopped working — it's still a royal palace, still guarded by soldiers, still home to the Yeoman Warders and their families who live inside these walls, and the Ceremony of the Keys, the locking-up ritual performed every single night, is said to have run unbroken for over 700 years. If you're continuing to Tower Bridge — and you should, it's a ten-minute walk east along the river — you'll see this fortress from its walkways, pale above the Thames, exactly as arriving prisoners saw it. Some views don't change in 900 years.
chapters.title: Wrap-Up — A Thousand Years in One Afternoon

intro: Welcome to the Tower of London — nearly a thousand years of English history packed inside one ring of walls on the north bank of the Thames. This has been a fortress, a royal palace, a prison, a mint, a menagerie, and the vault for the Crown Jewels, sometimes all at once. Our route is deliberate: we hit the Crown Jewels first, while the line is shortest, then work through the White Tower, the wall walk, the medieval palace, and the prison towers, finishing with the ravens on Tower Green. Give it a good two and a half hours, wear shoes you can climb spiral stairs in, and let's go make sense of the most storied castle in Britain.
mapNote: Think of the Tower as three concentric layers. The White Tower stands in the middle. Around it is the Inner Curtain Wall, studded with 13 towers — most of our stops (Bloody Tower, Beauchamp Tower, Medieval Palace, Torture exhibition) are in or on this wall, and the Wall Walk runs along its top, entered near the Salt Tower on the east side. Tower Green and the Chapel of St Peter ad Vincula sit in the open space west of the White Tower. The Jewel House is in the Waterloo Barracks, the long building along the north wall. Outside the inner wall is the Outer Curtain Wall and the (now grassy) moat; Traitors' Gate is on the river side, to the south. Our route: entrance at the southwest, straight north to the Jewel House, then the White Tower, up onto the east Wall Walk, down into the Medieval Palace on the south wall, then west and north through the prison towers to Tower Green.
practical: Go to the Crown Jewels FIRST, as this guide does. The Jewel House line is shortest in the first hour after opening and can stretch badly by midday.

Join a free Yeoman Warder ('Beefeater') tour — included with admission, about an hour, departing regularly from near the entrance. The Warders live here, guard the Tower, and deliver its bloodiest stories with stand-up comic timing. It's the best hour you'll spend on site.
The Crown Jewels are included in your entry ticket — no separate charge — but photography is not allowed inside the Jewel House.
Expect lots of stairs: the White Tower and wall walk involve steep, uneven, sometimes one-way spiral staircases. Step-free access is limited in the historic towers.
Budget at least 2.5–3 hours. Rushing the Tower is the classic mistake — the small towers and graffiti reward slow looking.
Traitors' Gate and the ravens are best seen as you walk the grounds between towers; keep an eye out for the Ravenmaster's talks near the raven enclosure on Tower Green.
The on-site cafés are fine for a break, but the walls themselves are the picnic spot — benches along the wall walk have Thames views.
subtitle: Fortress, palace, prison — and the Crown Jewels
title: Tower of London
